title: Ziembiński v. Poland (No. 2)
facts:
The applicant, born in 1944 and living in Kłomnice, is proprietor and editor-in-chief of the local weekly "Komu i Czemu", published in the Radomsko and Bełchatów Districts. In issue no. 33 of 18 August 2004 he published an article entitled "Elegantly wrapped dung" ("Łajno – elegancko opakowane"), which read, in so far as relevant:

"A poser is someone who does everything to produce external effects by his conduct, speech and, in particular, with the populism he preaches. He is a numbskull posing as the people's tribune. The only panacea, or universal cure, for such a person is to recognise his intentions and take up a bloodless fight using arguments. An argument against any kind of tricks by a poser or populist will be always a counter-argument based on reality, logic and the opportunity to put one's intentions into practice.
I remember when, not so long ago, the author of the proposal to develop a quail farm as a panacea against rural unemployment had a go at me in an accommodating local newspaper, accusing me of malice, a willingness to discredit every good idea, and mindlessness leading to nasty mental disease and many other irreversible disorders of the mind. At the same time he declared that he would continue doing his job, that is, condemning farmers to breeding nice little birds in order to collect their eggs. His boss considered the quail business very important, because it would eliminate the need for viagra. There has not been a sideshow like it in the Radomsko District for a long time. So the time is approaching when pilgrimages of men from all over Poland, and maybe even the European Union, will come to Radomsko to taste quail eggs and later begin procreating.
I wonder who has gone mad in the district, and why mad ideas, supported by even madder arguments, can be accepted by our officials. But no matter. Every dull boss can be convinced by any rubbish. Once more I want to authoritatively and responsibly declare that neither quail breeding, nor mushroom growing, nor Eternit [a registered trademark for fibre cement], which suddenly seems to have dropped out of the picture, will solve the unemployment problem in the villages of our region. And I will continue calling the actions of dim-witted officials and their dull bosses pretentious and populist, and no numbskull will convince me that I am wrong. ..."

The article then described in general terms a local economic development programme presented to the applicant by a businessman, and ended: "This is not a venture of the quail variety by some smart poser or populist who is able to sell his dull bosses dung nicely wrapped in words. And he actually sells it."

On 8 March 2005 M.D., the mayor of the Radomsko District (starosta), G.D., head and spokesperson of the district's marketing department, and K.H., an employee of that department, lodged a private bill of indictment with the Radomsko District Court accusing the applicant of defamation through the mass media under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code. They alleged that the copious use of words such as "numbskull", "dull boss", "dim-witted official", "poser" and "populist" ("palant", "nierozgarnięty szef", "przygłupawy urzędnik", "pozer", "populista") had defamed them as local government officials, lowered them in public opinion and undermined the public confidence necessary for their duties. They sought publication of an apology, reimbursement of costs and payment of PLN 5,000 to charity. The Radomsko District Court declined jurisdiction and transmitted the case to the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court, which held two hearings.

On 8 February 2006 the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court held that the use of "numbskull", "poser" and "dim-witted official" in respect of K.H., and "dull bosses" in respect of M.D. and G.D., amounted to insult (zniewaga) through the mass media under Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code. It convicted the applicant, fined him PLN 10,000 (approx. EUR 2,630) and ordered him to pay the private prosecutors' costs (PLN 900) and the State Treasury's costs (PLN 1,000). The court found that since March 2004 the newspaper had published articles critical of M.D. and his officials, particularly of K.H.'s initiative, in which G.D. was also involved, to develop quail farming to tackle local impoverishment; the applicant had published an ironic article on it in April 2004 and a journalist a detailed article in June 2004, and the conflict had intensified with each article. In the impugned article the applicant had decided once again to mock the two officials and their superior. The court rejected the applicant's argument that the article was a simple column in which any resemblance to real persons was coincidental, finding that it formed part of a campaign against the private prosecutors, who were easily identifiable owing to the publicity of the project and earlier articles.

The court held that a journalist may criticise public officials but may not use the media manipulatively to wage private wars, which was unethical, unprofessional and incompatible with the media's role of serving State and society. It stated: "The fair criticism and objective coverage, free from personal emotions, which is desired in journalism, gave way to the private interest of the defendant, pursued through expressions which, in common understanding, remain offensive and disrespectful. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word 'numbskull' ('palant') in the analysed context, although its literal meaning is legally irrelevant, fulfils all the criteria of insult within the meaning of Article 216 of the Criminal Code. Of an equally offensive character are the terms 'poser', 'dim-witted official' and 'dull boss'. It would be hard to find a person who would not feel offended by similar epithets, especially if formulated in the press." It added that the word "dung" in the title had a cruder equivalent, undoubtedly meant to describe K.H.'s contribution accepted by his "dull bosses", "dull" meaning not sharp, unintelligent, intellectually retarded. It found no grounds to hold that the words had lowered the prosecutors in public esteem or undermined confidence in them, so Article 212 § 2 did not apply; rather, the words harmed their perception of their dignity, which was the applicant's intention: "By using insulting words in respect of the district officials, Maciej Ziembiński intended to derive satisfaction from doing them moral harm." Acknowledging a conflict between constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and the right to reputation, it found the applicant's acts a blatant abuse of freedom of speech and professional ethics, as he had been settling a private conflict. It considered a prison sentence disproportionate and the fine proportionate to the gravity of the offence and his guilt.

The applicant appealed, contesting that the article concerned the private prosecutors personally, arguing that it sarcastically depicted people achieving personal gain by pretending to work and their dull bosses who accepted this, that criticism of the quail project was legitimate, and that public figures must accept harsh criticism. On 18 April 2006 the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court upheld the judgment and ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 in appeal costs. It endorsed the findings of fact and that the words were insulting and harmful to the prosecutors' dignity, holding that while fair criticism of public authorities was socially desirable and legally accepted, legal protection did not extend to insulting words offending human dignity. The judgment was served on 29 May 2006.

Relevant law: Articles 14, 31 § 3 and 54 § 1 of the Constitution guarantee press freedom and freedom of expression, subject to proportionate statutory limits. Article 216 § 1 of the Criminal Code penalises insult with a fine or restriction of liberty; § 2 penalises insult through the mass media with a fine, restriction of liberty or up to one year's imprisonment; prosecution is by private bill of indictment. In judgment P 10/06 (30 October 2006) the Constitutional Court upheld Article 212 §§ 1 and 2 as constitutional, finding that dignity and reputation may prevail over freedom of expression and that civil-law protection is not necessarily as effective as criminal-law protection. In SK 43/05 (12 May 2008) it held Article 213 § 2 unconstitutional in so far as it required a true allegation concerning a public official's conduct also to pursue a justifiable public interest.
applicantSubmissions: He had not harmed other people's good name or violated their rights; he had not even put the initials of the district officials in his article.

He had respected the principle of accuracy required of journalists under the Press Act; relying on the Constitutional Court's judgment of 12 May 2008, a person accused of insult should not be held liable if he complied with standards of accuracy and reliability in gathering and verifying information, even if the allegations proved false.

He had accurately reported on the quail farm project having been appropriated by local officials, and the interference with his right to present his opinion on negative phenomena in local life was unjustified; the Press Act and the Constitution enable free and independent media to criticise the exercise of power by local government.

He had not insulted any person, since he used no names or initials and criticised only methods and acts, without mentioning the office concerned; the words were not directed at anyone personally but at the problem of populist activity by the authorities and the supposed work of local officials.
Dictionaries did not list the words used as insulting expressions.
Public figures must accept the risk of being exposed to more severe criticism.

Journalistic criticism need not be devoid of personal feelings or emotional engagement; newspapers are not government bulletins recording only facts, and emotionless publications would not be read, so a journalist cannot be forced to write without emotional engagement.
The punishment was disproportionate, having led to the gradual economic downfall of the newspaper.
The limits of acceptable criticism in such a case should have been determined through civil rather than criminal law.
governmentSubmissions: The interference was prescribed by law, namely Article 216 of the Criminal Code, and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others.

While there is little scope under Article 10 § 2 for restrictions on political speech or debate on matters of public interest, the domestic courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons and thoroughly justified their finding that the applicant's statements amounted to insult.
The applicant overstepped the limits of acceptable criticism.

The fine of PLN 10,000 was calculated in the light of the applicant's financial situation; the courts chose not to impose restriction of liberty or imprisonment, and the penalty was the most lenient available and proportionate to his guilt and the social danger of his act.

The Constitutional Court (P 10/06 and SK 43/05) stressed that while freedom of expression is important, individual dignity must also be protected and may prevail; criminal-law protection of reputation and good name is not unconstitutional in itself, since the consequences of an attack on a person's good name cannot be reversed and later apologies cannot eradicate it.
The criminal proceedings were initiated by a private bill of indictment lodged by private individuals, not by a public prosecutor.
